+The safest starting point is to treat a published mark scheme as a **source document that contains atomic awardable units**, not as a free-text explanation of how to grade in general. +## Why the system needs separate evidence and taxonomy layers

+Official exam syllabuses are not written as clean knowledge graphs. In practice, that means a tutor should not collapse “what the syllabus explicitly says,” “what a question is trying to measure,” and “what internal teaching path the platform uses” into a single entity. citeturn21view0turn21view1turn21view2turn11view0

Cambridge syllabuses include paper scope, learning outcomes, command words, and entry/making-entries rules; AP frameworks include learning objectives, essential knowledge, and explicit exclusions; AQA distinguishes directly assessable subject content from other supporting material. citeturn16view0turn16view3turn27view1turn27view2turn17view1turn17view0turn15view1
+
+The `claim_force` field is essential. It should not be binary. A workable set is: `required`, `assessable`, `background_only`, `administrative`, `excluded_from_assessment`, and `illustrative_nonbinding`. This is necessary because boards frequently separate required content from examples or exclusions. AP Chemistry says essential knowledge is the required content associated with the learning objective assessed on the exam, while exclusion statements identify content that will not be assessed, though it may appear as background. AQA says the left column is assessable specification content and the right column is not assumed knowledge for assessment. citeturn17view1turn17view2turn15view1
+
+```mermaid
+flowchart LR
+    A[Official syllabus PDF or HTML] --> B[Source document record]
+    B --> C[Reviewed evidence object]
+    C --> D[Official scope graph]
+    C --> E[Topic taxonomy mappings]
+    E --> F[Questions]
+    E --> G[Learning objects]
+    E --> H[Review tasks]
+    C --> I[Boundary claims engine]
+```
+
+A concise recommended shape is:
+
+```json
+{
+  "syllabus_evidence_id": "sev_AP-CHEM_2024_v1_topic_7.6_A1",
+  "source_document_id": "src_AP-CHEM_CED_2024_v1",
+  "official_text": "When a reaction is reversed, K is inverted.",
+  "evidence_type": "essential_knowledge",
+  "claim_force": "required",
+  "applies_to": {
+    "issuer": "College Board",
+    "qualification": "AP Chemistry",
+    "subject_code": null,
+    "syllabus_version": "2024 V.1",
+    "unit_ref": "7",
+    "topic_ref": "7.6",
+    "learning_objective_ref": "7.6.A",
+    "paper_scope": "full exam"
+  },
+  "anchor": {
+    "source_url": "official document URL",
+    "text_quote_selector": {
+      "exact": "When a reaction is reversed, K is inverted."
+    },
+    "text_position_selector": {
+      "start": 6032,
+      "end": 6033
+    },
+    "page": 140
+  },
+  "provenance": {
+    "review_status": "approved",
+    "reviewed_by": "syllabus reviewer",
+    "reviewed_at": "2026-07-01T00:00:00Z",
+    "derived_from": "src_AP-CHEM_CED_2024_v1"
+  },
+  "superseded_by": null
+}
+```
+
+The important design choice is that the evidence object stores **verbatim official wording plus normalized scope metadata**, not just an interpreted paraphrase. CASE explicitly treats the `fullStatement` as the official statement defined by the issuing agency. That should be your standard for syllabus-bound evidence as well. citeturn6view3turn25view0
+
+## Topic taxonomy and syllabus linkage model
+
+The topic taxonomy should be a separate, product-owned graph. It should not be a mirror of official syllabus wording, and it should not pretend to be official when it is not. College Board’s AP Biology syllabus development guidance explicitly allows a course to organize required content using a different approach or sequence from the official framework, as long as it clearly indicates where each required unit’s content is taught. CASE likewise supports derived framework documents and normalization nodes that exist to organize the hierarchy even when they are not themselves the official target of alignment. citeturn14view0turn7view1turn25view0
+
+That means the taxonomy can and should contain pedagogically useful nodes that official documents often omit, such as `procedure`, `subskill`, `prerequisite`, `common_confusion`, `representation_type`, and `question_family`. CASE itself allows flexible item types and supports normalization nodes where needed for hierarchy construction. AP frameworks also separate course content from practices and suggested skills, which is another sign that a well-run learning product should model more than one axis. citeturn25view0turn19view1turn18view0
+
+The cleanest linkage pattern is to treat each taxonomy node as having one of three evidence relationships:
+
+- **Directly evidenced**: the node corresponds closely to an official statement, outcome, or paper scope.
+- **Derived but bounded**: the node is a decomposition or recombination of official scope for teaching purposes.
+- **Unbound enrichment**: the node is useful for learning, but not official syllabus scope.
+
+That distinction matters because only the first category can support strong syllabus-bound claims. The second can support internal navigation and learning design. The third must be visibly labeled as enrichment or prerequisite support, not exam scope. This is exactly the kind of distinction implied by AP exclusions, AQA’s assessable-vs-illustrative split, and the testing standards’ requirement to distinguish the tested domain from the broader target domain. citeturn17view1turn15view1turn11view0
+
+A good linkage model for a taxonomy node therefore includes: a stable taxonomy ID, a canonical path, a display label, a pedagogical description, evidence links, prerequisite links, and publication metadata. Evidence links should be typed. The most useful link types are `supported_by`, `bounded_by`, `excluded_by`, `paper_scoped_by`, `command_word_scoped_by`, and `replaced_by`. CASE’s association vocabulary is useful here because it already includes `isChildOf`, `precedes`, `exactMatchOf`, and `replacedBy`. citeturn25view0
+
+Questions, learning objects, procedure models, and review tasks should each link **both** to taxonomy nodes and to evidence objects. QTI is relevant here because it explicitly separates item/test content from results/reporting, and ECD is relevant because it distinguishes task models from evidence models and student models. In practical terms, `question_type` and `procedure_model` are product-side entities; they are usually not official syllabus entities. They should never be mistaken for official scope just because many questions in a syllabus happen to use them. citeturn13view0turn21view1turn21view2
+
+A question record should therefore include at least: `question_id`, `question_type`, `target_taxonomy_nodes`, `target_syllabus_evidence`, `context_evidence`, `exclusion_conflicts`, `paper_scope`, `command_word_profile`, and `procedure_models_used`. A review task should similarly link to the evidence it is meant to rehearse, not only to a broad topic bucket. Cambridge’s command word tables and paper details show why this is valuable: the same topic can be assessed in different ways under different papers or command words, and those differences are official. citeturn27view1turn27view2turn16view0
+
+## Versioning and migration strategy
+
+Official syllabus versioning and taxonomy versioning should be separate release lines. This is not optional. CASE’s versioning guidance says new framework versions can be managed with new CFDocument definitions, and deprecated documents should be locked to preserve historical reference. Cambridge’s own documents show why this matters: later versions can change wording, paper guidance, formulas, functions, learning outcomes, subject codes, and assessment structure. citeturn7view0turn7view2turn26view0turn26view1turn26view2

+# Atomic Mark Scheme Dependency Logic for Mathematics Exam Tutoring
+
+## What the evidence says and why one row is not enough
+
+Published mathematics mark schemes are real authority sources, but they are not self-sufficient as standalone scoring engines. AQA states that a mark scheme is a **working document**, expanded during standardisation, and that alternative answers not already covered are discussed and “legislated for”; unusual answers after standardisation must be referred to the Lead Examiner. Cambridge says its published scheme is an **aid** showing the basis on which examiners were instructed, but it does **not** include the discussions about alternative answers and should be read with the question paper and the Principal Examiner Report. OCR says much the same: its published scheme does not include the pre-marking discussions, unexpected correct methods must be credited fairly, and the scheme should be read with the question paper and report. Pearson likewise says exemplification may be limited and that doubtful cases must be referred to the team leader. These statements are the clearest reason a tutoring system must not treat one public row of a mark scheme as the whole truth of “why you lost this mark.” citeturn26view0turn18view0turn25view0turn25view1
+
+A second reason is structural. Public maths mark schemes encode only fragments of the real decision logic: mark type, a candidate-visible target, and terse notes like `dep`, `ft`, `oe`, `ISW`, `SC`, or `their`. But official instructions also depend on multiple-response policy, answer-line policy, whether method must be shown, whether the earlier mark can be **implied**, whether follow-through is allowed only on particular downstream marks, whether a correct value was spoiled by a later wrong argument, and whether a later part must reference a candidate’s earlier answer even if that answer is outside the current marking window. AQA explicitly distinguishes “choice” handling and says to award marks across the student’s **best attempts**, but withhold final accuracy/conclusion marks if complete answers conflict. Pearson instead says that if multiple uncrossed attempts remain, examiners should generally mark the **final answer that is the most complete**. OCR says to mark the **last attempt** unless it merely repeats part of the first attempt or is substantially less complete. Cambridge older specimen guidance says if two or more methods are offered, mark the method that leads to the **answer on the answer line**. A single raw row does not capture those board-level selection rules. citeturn26view0turn25view1turn17view0turn19view0
+
+A third reason is that marks are often not local to one line of work. Cambridge’s current notes define dependent marks as `DM/DB`, explain that earlier marks can be **implied** when steps are run together, and restrict `FT` to the indicated A or B marks. OCR uses `dep*`, explains that method marks may be independent in principle, and says that sometimes later parts must use answers from earlier parts even if those answers are not fully visible in the current image zone. SQA’s guidance reaches the same conclusion from another direction: after an error, later working must still be checked, but only if it has a similar level of difficulty; the appearance of a correct final answer does not by itself mean all marks are earned. So “why did I lose this mark?” is usually a question about a **dependency graph over candidate state**, not about one row in isolation. citeturn16view3turn17view0turn27view3
+
+For tutoring, the practical conclusion is strict: the system can explain **published criteria** and can offer **formative likelihoods**, but it should not present its decision as official scoring unless it is operating inside an authorized board workflow with the board’s standardisation, escalation, and reviewer procedures. OCR requires training packages, practice responses, and standardisation responses before live marking; Cambridge’s generic principles refer to standardisation scripts; AQA says standardisation ensures common application; Pearson requires escalation to the team leader when in doubt. A public tutoring product cannot honestly collapse those processes into a single deterministic mark row. citeturn25view0turn18view0turn26view0turn25view1
+
+![AQA AS Mathematics mark-type and abbreviation key from a 2024 official mark scheme.](turn13view0)
+
+## Recommended mark_scheme_item schema
+
+The core design choice should be to separate **surface notation** from **normalized semantics**. Boards use different visible labels for closely related ideas: AQA AS/A level uses `M`, `R`, `A`, `B`, `E`, and `F`; OCR uses `M`, `A`, `B`, `E`, `dep*`, `FT`, `ISW`, and `DR`; Cambridge uses `M`, `A`, `B`, `DM/DB`, `FT`, `isw`, and sometimes `nfww`; WJEC adds families such as `m`, `S`, `E`, `U`, `P`, `C`, `OC`, and `W`; Pearson A level guidance uses `M`, `A`, `B` plus abbreviations like `dep`, `ft`, `oe`, `SC`, `cso`, and `isw`. So the schema should always keep both `board_surface_label` and a `normalized_type`. citeturn26view0turn16view2turn16view3turn14view0turn25view1

+  "id": "q10b.alt1.item2",
+  "board": "AQA",
+  "qualification": "AS Mathematics 7356/2",
+  "series": "2024-06",
+  "question_ref": "10(b)",
+  "part_ref": "10(b)",
+  "path_id": "alt1",
+  "board_surface_label": "M1dep",
+  "normalized_type": "method_dependent",
+  "mark_value": 1,

+  "criterion_text": "their 8d = 28 + their 20 or 8d = 48",
+  "official_source_ref": "turn24view0",
+
+  "assessment_objectives": ["AO1.1a"],
+  "supported_claim_ids": ["claim.solve_linear_step_2"],
+
+  "dependency_ids": ["q10b.alt1.item1"],
+  "follow_through_policy_id": "ft.from.previous_incorrect_result",
+  "attempt_selection_policy_id": "board.aqa.choice_policy",
+  "conflict_policy_id": "withhold_final_accuracy_if_conflicting_complete_answers",
+
+  "accepted_variant_ids": ["variant.oe", "variant.their_nonzero_guard"],
+  "special_case_ids": [],
+  "alternative_group_id": "q10b.methods",
+  "mutually_exclusive_with": ["alt2.bundle"],
+
+  "requires_explicit_working": true,
+  "can_be_implied": false,
+  "ignore_subsequent_working": false,
+  "not_from_wrong_working": false,
+
+  "diagnostic_rule_ids": ["diag.missing_dependency", "diag.follow_through_used"],
+  "uncertainty_rule_ids": ["unclear_which_attempt", "unvalidated_method"],
+  "authority_tier": "published_official_criterion"
+}
+```

+That object needs six companion structures.
+
+A `supported_claim` should represent the actual thing being credited, not the mark token. For example: “forms the equation \(7c+5t=480\)”, “shows that their non-prime value factorises”, “states a valid reason involving the area under the graph”, or “draws a straight line of best fit”. This aligns with official practice because exam boards often describe marks in terms of **claims or steps**, not just final answers. AQA’s R marks are for reasoning and E marks for explanation; WJEC explicitly distinguishes strategy, explanation, units, plotting, curves, and organizing/communicating; OCR’s E1 is for explaining or establishing a result. A claim-centric model is therefore closer to the real marking unit than a raw label-centric model. citeturn26view0turn14view0turn16view2
+
+An `accepted_variant` should hold the admissible expression space for that claim: exact match, algebraic equivalence, allowed rounding range, notation convention, diagram tolerance, or board-condoned form. This is needed because boards explicitly publish `OE`, `ACF`, `AWRT`, `AWFW`, `rot`, and diagram tolerances, and because Cambridge and OCR both mention that there may be several equally acceptable intermediate forms. citeturn26view0turn16view2turn17view0turn25view0
+
+A `scoring_rule` should say when the mark is awardable. A `diagnostic_rule` should say how to explain the most likely reason it was not awarded. Keeping those separate matters because a tutoring system often has to say “I cannot tell whether this official mark would be awarded” even when it can still say “the likely missing prerequisite is the earlier method step.” That distinction matches the official documents, which repeatedly instruct examiners to escalate doubtful cases rather than improvise. citeturn26view0turn25view0turn25view1
+
+## Dependency and follow-through model
+
+The dependency model should be a **typed directed graph**, not a simple parent pointer. At minimum, it needs `requires_awarded`, `requires_implied`, `depends_on_previous_part`, `allows_follow_through_from`, `conflicts_with`, and `alternative_to`. That structure is directly motivated by official usage: Cambridge uses `DM/DB`; OCR uses `dep*`; WJEC uses lowercase `m` for dependent method marks; AQA uses dependent M marks and explicit `their`/`ft`; Pearson uses `dep` and `ft`. These are all dependency edges, but they are not the same kind of edge. citeturn16view3turn16view2turn14view0turn26view0turn25view1

Cambridge current notes and OCR both say `FT` usually applies only to the indicated **A or B** marks, not automatically to everything downstream. OCR further notes that when a later part depends on an earlier part, the marker must refer back to the previous answer even if it is outside the current image zone. WJEC examples add guards such as “FT … provided π has been used in its calculation.” So a good `follow_through_policy` needs fields such as `source_result_selector`, `strictness`, `allowed_downstream_mark_types`, `preconditions`, and `error_classes_carried`. citeturn19view0turn16view3turn25view0turn24view1
+

+{
+  "id": "ft.from.previous_incorrect_result",
+  "source_result_selector": {
+    "kind": "candidate_result",
+    "from_part": "10(b).alt1.item1",
+    "binding": "their_answer"
+  },
+  "strictness": "normal",
+  "allowed_downstream_mark_types": ["accuracy", "independent"],
+  "preconditions": ["source_result_exists", "source_result_is_coherent"],
+  "disallowed_if": ["wrong_argument_passes_through_correct_value", "conflicting_final_answers"],
+  "carry_error_classes": ["numerical_slip", "algebraic_slip"],
+  "do_not_carry": ["method_absence_when_method_required", "forbidden_transform", "invalid_reasoning"]
+}
+```

AQA defines `their` as credit from a previous incorrect result, and OCR says later parts may need the earlier answer even if it is not visible at the current location. +

That means the state machine needs at least three states: `correct_and_final`, `correct_but_subsequently_spoiled_ignored`, and `correct_value_seen_inside_invalid_argument`. Without that distinction, a tutor will over-award marks whenever a candidate briefly writes a correct value and then reasons incorrectly from it. citeturn18view0turn17view0turn25view0
+

+

+

SQA’s horizontal/vertical marking says to choose whichever method **benefits the candidate**, but not a combination of both. Pearson usually says mark the **final answer that is the most complete**; OCR usually says mark the **last attempt** unless it is merely partial or less complete; older Cambridge guidance says mark the method that leads to the **answer line** answer. So the product should implement `attempt_selection_policy` as a board-specific strategy object, not a universal “best of everything” rule. citeturn26view0turn27view2turn25view1turn17view0turn19view0
